newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: Russian military, Tajiks review Afghan strategy.
newsitem.headline: Russian military, Tajiks review Afghan strategy.

text.p: The Russian border guards who defend Tajikistan began a meeting on Saturday to work out a strategy against the spread of militant Islam from Afghanistan.

General Andrei Nikolayev, who commands Russia's Border Guard Service, opened the council in the Tajik capital Dushanbe saying it had been prompted by "the aggravated situation on the Tajik-Afghan border and the progress of the Taleban movement".
"The Russian president (Boris Yeltsin) is watching developments in the Central Asian region closely," he said.
The purist Taleban militia has installed strict Sharia law in Afghanistan and controls most of its territory, except for the north, bordering Tajikistan.

Russia and the five former Soviet states in Central Asia are worried that a wave of radical Islam and instability may spread across their frontiers if the Taleban mount a successful summer campaign against the forces of General Abdul Rashid Dostum and Ahmad Shah Masood, who now control northern Afghanistan.

Around 20,000 Russian peacekeepers and border guards are deployed in Tajikistan. Russia, which is separated from Tajikistan by over 1,000 km (700 miles) of Kazakh territory, sees them as a buffer against the spread of militant Islam.
Nikolayev said the border guards were worried by a possible massive influx of refugees from northern Afghanistan in the case of an escalation of fighting there.
Tajik President Imomali Rakhmonov told the council said that more than a million refugees could pour into Tajikistan.
Nikolayev said that "uncontrollable groups of the united Tajik opposition" was another major concern.
Tajikistan's secular government and the country's Islamist opposition agreed last year on a ceasefire in their four-year civil war, in which tens of thousands of people died.
The relative peace has, however, been disturbed by armed bands operating from their bases in Afghanistan.
"All this may lead to a sharp aggravation of the situation in the Central Asian region," Nikolayev said.
Rakhmonov said: "Decisive measures must be taken to defend and keep peace".
The Tajik president asked Nikolayev to render assistance to his country's border guards.

Kazakhstan sent a representative but the other former Soviet Central Asian -- Kyrgyzstan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan -- declined to take part in the council, which Moscow had hoped would work out a joint strategy against threats to stability.
